title: India's 7.8% GDP Growth Faces Scrutiny Over Methods and Meaning
excerpt: A former finance secretary, an ex-RBI governor, and a business strategist all question what India's headline growth number captures — and what it leaves out.
body:
• India's April-June GDP growth of 7.8% beat forecasts but triggered a debate over revised base-year data and the accuracy of price deflators
  • Former finance secretary Subhash Chandra Garg argued the figure was inflated by downward revisions to year-ago data, while ex-RBI governor Raghuram Rajan questioned why strong GDP has not translated into more jobs and investment
  • The statistics ministry defended its methodology, citing a new Producer Price Index with over 300 deflators and additional data sources
  • Business strategist Vivek Singhal argues the deeper issue is that GDP alone cannot measure human capability and sustainable prosperity

The Numbers That Sparked the Fight

India's economy grew 7.8% in the April-June quarter, comfortably beating the 7.1% forecast by analysts in a Reuters poll. Investment and manufacturing strength added to solid consumer demand, making the world's fifth-largest economy one of the fastest-growing major markets. But the number itself has become the subject of a multi-front debate spanning politics, economics, and philosophy.

Subhash Chandra Garg, a former top Finance Ministry bureaucrat, argued that the growth figure was inflated because the government had reduced its measure of GDP for the year-earlier period — the basis of comparison. Under the old GDP series, nominal growth for the same quarter would have been just 2.6%, not the 10.3% the government reported, according to Reuters.

Rajan Raises Broader Concerns

Former Reserve Bank of India Governor Raghuram Rajan added a different dimension. In a television interview, he asked why robust GDP growth was not showing up in stronger job creation, domestic investment, or foreign portfolio inflows.

Rajan later clarified on LinkedIn that he had not questioned or endorsed the specific GDP numbers. His concern, he said, was broader: why strong headline growth had not translated over time into more private investment, foreign investment, and decent jobs.

India's opposition Congress party seized on the controversy, with general secretary Jairam Ramesh calling the 7.8% figure "statistical gymnastics."

Government Defends the Data

The statistics ministry pushed back. Statistics Secretary Saurabh Garg told reporters that the revisions reflected a new GDP series with a 2022-23 base year, incorporating updated data sources and methodology — not systematic bias.

The new series uses a Producer Price Index with more than 300 deflators for inputs and outputs, up from about 180 previously, providing more granular price information. The government said quarterly revisions over the past three years had moved in both directions, and annual changes had been relatively small.

Some private economists have questioned whether the deflator — at 2.3% for the April-June quarter — understated inflation compared with retail inflation above 4% and wholesale inflation over 9%. The government argues its double-deflation method, which separately adjusts output values and input costs, is globally accepted.

"The recent debate over India's GDP numbers should be understood as more than a statistical controversy. It raises a deeper question for 21st-century economics: what exactly are we trying to maximise?"

— Vivek Singhal, Founder and CEO, Strategic Business Management Co

Beyond the Statistical Argument

Vivek Singhal, a business strategist and author, argues in NDTV that the entire debate is missing a larger point. In his view, GDP should be "one dial on the dashboard — not the entire dashboard."

Singhal, an IIT Delhi alumnus whose recent book "Dominion and Dharma" was released on India's Independence Day, distinguishes between what he calls "Dominion Capitalism" — focused on production, ownership, and capture — and "Dharma Capitalism," which asks how capital, markets, and technology can expand human capability while creating sustainable prosperity.

"A confident India should be able to recognise strong economic momentum and, at the same time, welcome rigorous scrutiny of methodology, revisions and transparency," Singhal told NDTV. "These are not contradictory positions. Trust in economic statistics is itself a form of national capital."

Mixed Signals in the Data

High-frequency indicators largely support the growth narrative. Auto sales rose 21% in August, bank credit sits at a decade-high 19%, and India's net direct tax revenue climbed more than 23% year-on-year in the April-August period, according to Reuters.

But the Purchasing Managers' Index, a survey-based measure, has weakened to multiyear lows — a disconnect that keeps the debate alive.

What to Watch

A separate Reuters Breakingviews analysis published September 8 noted that while the credibility of India's headline GDP figure has "significantly improved," recent revisions do not go far enough to reduce unnecessary surprises. More transparency on data inputs remains the key demand from economists and market participants watching the $4 trillion economy.
nri_angle: India's GDP methodology debate carries investment and portfolio implications for diaspora investors tracking the $4 trillion economy.
